topics.title: 16.1.1 Comparing vector, deque, and list
topics.summary: A vector provides contiguous element storage and efficient indexed access. A deque provides indexed access with a different, non-contiguous overall storage organization and efficient operations at both ends. A list provides linked bidirectional traversal and node-oriented insertion or removal at known positions.

cards.question: Explain Comparing vector, deque, and list in your own words.
cards.answer: A vector provides contiguous element storage and efficient indexed access. A deque provides indexed access with a different, non-contiguous overall storage organization and efficient operations at both ends. A list provides linked bidirectional traversal and node-oriented insertion or removal at known positions.

blocks.text: The standard specifies behavior and complexity without requiring every implementation to use one exact internal layout. In particular, do not infer a portable deque block size or a list node’s byte size from one debugger session. Such observations can explain a measured implementation but are not the container’s universal contract.

blocks.text: A vector’s contiguous storage supports efficient traversal and indexed access. It often makes a good default for owned sequences because elements are close together and the representation is compact. Inserting in the middle can shift later elements, and growth can reallocate. Those are predictable tradeoffs to evaluate against the workload rather than reasons to reject vectors categorically.

blocks.text: A deque supports efficient growth at both ends and random access, but its overall storage is not one contiguous array. Code that assumes &deque[0] + i reaches every element is not using its documented model. A list provides node-based bidirectional traversal and operations such as splicing under the appropriate allocator conditions, but each node has storage and indirection costs.

blocks.text: The right comparison includes finding a position. A list can insert near a known iterator without shifting unrelated elements, but finding the tenth-thousandth element by repeated traversal is not constant time. A vector may outperform a list for many practical workloads despite a less favorable isolated insertion complexity because traversal and locality dominate. Measure a representative sequence of operations, not only the one operation that makes a preferred container look best.

topics.title: 16.1.2 Evaluating Insertion and Access Costs
topics.summary: List insertion at an already known valid position can avoid shifting later elements, but locating that position may require linear traversal. Vector insertion in the middle moves later elements, while appending can be amortized constant time across growth. Count lookup, allocation, element movement, and subsequent traversal together.

blocks.text: Stable references can justify a node-based structure even when raw traversal is slower. Conversely, a dense read-heavy workload often benefits from contiguous storage. Use complexity to eliminate obviously unsuitable designs, then benchmark representative complete operations rather than an isolated instruction chosen to favor one container.

blocks.text: Separate access, insertion, erasure, allocation, and movement costs. A vector lookup by index is constant time, but finding a record by an arbitrary ID requires a search unless another index is maintained. A list insertion at a known position has a different cost from searching for that position. A deque’s end operations differ from its middle operations.

blocks.text: Handle stability can be more important than the smallest asymptotic expression. A subsystem that retains references across insertions may need a representation or indirection strategy that preserves them. Another subsystem can avoid the requirement by retaining stable IDs and reacquiring records. Changing the interface can sometimes remove a costly representation constraint more effectively than changing the container.

blocks.text: Memory usage includes more than element payload. Node links, allocation metadata, spare vector capacity, hash buckets, and alignment all contribute. For a thousand tiny records, per-node overhead can be substantial relative to the data. For a few expensive objects requiring stable addresses, an extra level of ownership indirection may be reasonable. Use the actual element type and expected population in the analysis.

blocks.text: Ordered associative containers maintain key order according to a comparator. Their notion of key equivalence comes from that comparator, not necessarily from operator==. Two keys can be equivalent when neither compares before the other. If a case-insensitive comparator treats two spellings as equivalent, a set will not store them as distinct keys merely because their byte strings differ.

blocks.text: A comparator must remain a valid ordering relation for the stored keys. Mutating external comparator state so that existing keys would order differently can invalidate the container’s assumptions. Likewise, a key cannot be casually modified in place through an ordinary map iterator. The container’s structure depends on the ordering relationship used when elements were placed.

topics.title: 16.2.2 Comparing Hash-Based Containers
topics.summary: An unordered map uses a hash to organize candidate locations and equality to decide key matches. Equal keys must produce compatible hash values under the container’s requirements. Average constant-time lookup depends on hashing and workload conditions; worst-case behavior can be linear.

blocks.text: Iteration order is not a sorted-order contract and may change after rehashing or between implementations. Rehashing also has iterator consequences distinct from element-reference rules. Use an ordered container or sort a separate result when output order is a requirement. Reserve and load-factor tuning can reduce avoidable rehashing but do not repair a poor or adversarial hash policy.

A service with strict timing or untrusted key concerns needs a workload-specific analysis rather than the sentence “hash maps are constant time.” The book’s small fixtures use ordinary keys and do not claim denial-of-service resistance from the container choice.

Iteration order is not a stable output contract. Rehashing, insertion history, library implementation, or key distribution can change it. A report that requires reproducibility should collect keys or records and sort them by an explicit rule before publication. Tests should check membership and values for unordered storage, not one accidental traversal order.

Rehash affects iterators differently from references and pointers to existing elements. Erasure has its own rules. Reuse the operation-specific reasoning from Chapter 15 rather than assuming a hash table behaves like a vector. For application identity, a key-based lookup often communicates the intent more directly than retaining an iterator through unrelated mutations.
